summary: Seated on a rock beside Jacob's well, the young, haloed Christ in a purple mantle raises his hand in speech towards the Samaritan woman, who draws water with a rope from the well-head under its wooden frame. A disciple in white stands behind him. One of the miracle and teaching scenes high on the north wall of Theodoric's palace church, it distils a long Gospel dialogue about 'living water' into a single quiet encounter.
facts: The thirteen scenes of the north wall show Christ's miracles and teaching; in all of them he appears young and beardless, robed in imperial purple.
The scenes were not arranged in biblical order but are thought to follow the Gospel readings of the Lenten liturgy in Theodoric's palace church.

summary: Christ, young and beardless in a purple robe, sits enthroned between two angels: a red-clad angel stands beside the sheep at his right hand, a blue-clad angel beside the goats at his left. The image turns the parable of the Last Judgement into a calm, symmetrical vision of Christ as judge and shepherd, one of the earliest monumental images of the judgement in Christian art.
facts: Because the angel beside the goats is clothed in blue, some art historians have identified him as the earliest depiction of Satan (or a fallen angel) in Western art, though this reading is debated.

summary: Christ, haloed and in purple, reaches out to touch the eyes of a blind man with a staff, while a second blind man stands beside him and an apostle in white follows behind. The figures stand on a strip of green ground against the gold, framed by the jewelled border common to the whole cycle. The scene presents Christ as the light-giver who opens the eyes of those who call to him.

summary: The healed man strides away with his bed strapped to his back while Christ, haloed in purple and followed by a disciple, raises his hand in blessing and command. The mosaicists showed the moment just after the miracle, when Christ's word 'Rise, take up thy bed, and walk' has already done its work.
facts: The thirteen scenes of the north wall show Christ's miracles and teaching; in all of them he appears young and beardless, robed in imperial purple.
The cycle contains two healings of paralytics: this one at the pool of Bethesda, and another at Capernaum in which the sick man is let down through the roof.

summary: Lazarus, still wrapped in his grave-clothes, stands in the doorway of a small temple-like tomb at the top of a flight of steps, as Christ, haloed and in purple, stretches out his hand to call him forth, a disciple at his side. summary: At the crown of the great arch before the presbytery, a bearded Christ with long dark hair looks out from a gold-rimmed medallion, holding a book, flanked by medallions of the apostles. Set within a band of twining ornament, he presides over the chain of saints that runs down both sides of the arch. The mature, bearded type seen here contrasts with the youthful Christ enthroned on the globe in the apse just beyond.
facts: The intrados of the triumphal arch carries fifteen medallions: Christ, the Twelve Apostles and Saints Gervasius and Protasius, traditionally the sons of Saint Vitalis.
The decoration of San Vitale was begun under Bishop Ecclesius (c. 525) and the church was consecrated in 547 or 548 under Bishop Maximian.

summary: At the crown of the presbytery vault, a white haloed Lamb stands against a dark blue sky scattered with gold stars, enclosed in a wreath of leaves, fruit and flowers. The wreath is upheld by four angels standing on globes (not visible in this detail), so that the whole vault converges on Christ as the sacrificial Lamb directly above the altar.
facts: The cross-ribbed vault is covered with acanthus scrolls, birds and animals, all converging on the wreath that frames the Lamb.
Placing the Lamb above the altar linked the image to the Eucharist celebrated beneath it, a theme continued in the lunettes of Abel, Melchizedek and Abraham on the presbytery walls.

summary: In a round medallion at the summit of the triumphal arch, a bearded Christ raises his right hand in blessing and holds a jewelled book in his left. He floats in a sea of red and blue clouds, flanked by the winged symbols of the evangelists, here the man of Matthew and the lion of Mark. The image crowns the arch above the sixth-century apse with its great jewelled cross of the Transfiguration.
facts: The four winged creatures around Christ are the symbols of the evangelists: eagle (John), man (Matthew), lion (Mark) and calf (Luke).
Below them, twelve lambs, symbols of the apostles, issue from the jewelled cities of Jerusalem and Bethlehem.
The church was consecrated on 9 May 549 by Bishop Maximian, but the arch mosaics belong to later campaigns of decoration.

summary: Within a blue roundel ringed in white and red, a youthful, beardless Christ with a fringe of brown hair and a cross-inscribed halo looks directly at the viewer. The medallion sits at the crown of one of the chapel's arches amid the gold, heading a series of medallions of apostles and saints. This gentle, frontal image of the young Christ complements the warrior Christ who tramples the beasts above the chapel's entrance.
facts: The chapel was built as a private oratory of the bishops of Ravenna by Archbishop Peter II shortly after 495, and was originally dedicated to the Saviour.
ICOMOS described it as the only Early Christian private oratory to survive, notable for its strongly anti-Arian imagery.
